judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Breathless exclamations, the odd '!?' and a slightly clumsy subjunctive ('were not thrown into the fray') are pure Westwood; the plot stakes are loud and the journal entry is bare.

items.label: B
items.critique: Clipped modern fragments ('Very grim.', 'Not all of them.') read as deliberate literary craft; the 'X tells me you are the one' hand-off and 'get what you need in town' shape is a template.

items.label: C
items.critique: Far too long and too well-furnished with economic cause and effect (millers, ferrymen, farmers' sons); Westwood's quest-givers rarely world-build this densely, and the 'Never in all my years' line imitates rather than is.

items.label: D
items.critique: Practical, specific, slightly awkward ('safest way in for a [Group]'), with a reminder that explains the spells' use; the low-key 'Good luck and good speed' sounds like the original.

items.label: E
items.critique: Same skeleton as B and H: 'Grave news, lad', a named person vouching for you, a key/gate, a shopping reminder, and the reminder 'Those Zombies get bolder every night' is nearly verbatim from B.

items.label: F
items.critique: The drill-sergeant bluster is lively, but 'This cannot stand!' and the gold-potions-sword kit plus 'do not come back until' feel assembled from the same opening template.

items.label: G
items.critique: Stiff, formal, oddly punctuated ('The Master for the [Place].') and a capitalised 'YOU' in the reminder; the plain procedural journal is Westwood's habit.

items.label: H
items.critique: Tidy three-beat setup (vouched-for arrival, disaster, take this item and go) with an evocative 'every furnace has gone cold' image; polished and symmetrical in a way Westwood's openings are not.

items.label: I
items.critique: Wordy, Latinate ('transpiring', 'antiquated records', 'furnish the answers'), with a grammar slip ('incursions ... is') and an empty page break; exactly the original's uneven mentor voice.

items.label: J
items.critique: Idioms used a little loosely ('rest on laurels'), 'Now, off with you!', and a plot-linking reminder that points to another person rather than restating the danger.

tells: The new texts share one opening template: a greeting of bad news ('Grave news, lad'), a third party who vouched for the hero, a concrete disaster with a night-time escalation, an item handed over, and a pointer to shops or supplies.

Reminders in the new texts restate atmosphere ('X get bolder every night', 'grows colder') and even repeat each other almost word for word; Westwood's reminders give a practical tip, a next person to find, or a plain 'Go quickly!'.

Westwood's prose is uneven: grammar slips, '!?', capitalised emphasis, stiff formal fragments, Latinate words in a mentor's mouth, and blank page breaks. The new texts are cleaner and more controlled, with crafted short fragments and vivid sensory images.
The new texts over-explain consequences (economy, guards' backgrounds, furnaces, mines falling silent); Westwood states the threat and the order with little texture beyond exclamation.
Westwood's journal entries are terse and sometimes vaguer than the dialogue ('Retrieve the [Thing].'); the new ones tend to restate the full objective with location and verb.
